title: Myelin Disorders
subject: Pathology
summary: Myelin insulates nerve fibres, enabling rapid conduction. Damage to myelin causes neurologic deficits that vary by location and cause. In low‑resource settings, infections and nutritional deficiencies are common triggers.

sections.p: Myelin is a lipid‑rich sheath produced by oligodendrocytes in the CNS and Schwann cells in the PNS. Loss or dysfunction of myelin (demyelination) is diagnosed by clinical pattern, neuro‑imaging (when available), and supportive laboratory tests.
b: CNS demyelination: multiple sclerosis, ADEM, HIV‑associated leukoencephalopathy
PNS demyelination: Guillain‑Barré syndrome (GBS), chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP)
Nutritional: vitamin B12, B6, folate deficiency

sections.p: Severity is graded by functional impact and extent of lesions.
b: Mild: isolated sensory loss or mild weakness
Moderate: gait disturbance, bladder dysfunction, or need for walking aid
Severe: quadriplegia, respiratory failure, or rapid progression (e.g., GBS)

sections.p: In East African hospitals the most frequent precipitants are infections and nutritional deficits.
b: Infectious: HIV, TB meningitis, malaria cerebral, schistosomiasis (spinal cord lesions)
Autoimmune: GBS after Campylobacter or viral infection, MS (less common)
Nutritional: vitamin B12 deficiency (vegetarian diet, malabsorption), B6 excess, folate deficiency
Toxins: lead, nitrous oxide abuse, herbal remedies with neurotoxic compounds

sections.p: Presentation depends on CNS vs PNS involvement and lesion level.
b: CNS: optic neuritis, limb weakness, sensory level, ataxia, bladder dysfunction
PNS (GBS): ascending symmetric weakness, areflexia, paresthesiae, facial weakness, possible respiratory compromise
B12 deficiency: peripheral neuropathy, dorsal column loss (proprioception), spastic paresis, megaloblastic anemia

t.b: Detects focal demyelinating lesions; helps differentiate MS/ADEM from infections
Looks for oligoclonal bands (MS) or elevated protein with normal cell count (GBS)
Screens for infectious triggers when imaging unavailable

sections.p: Identify patients who need urgent care.
b: Rapidly progressive weakness leading to respiratory failure (GBS)
Severe optic neuritis with vision loss
Bladder retention or incontinence indicating spinal cord involvement
Unexplained seizures in demyelinating disease

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, then provide disease‑specific therapy and supportive care.
b: Infectious trigger: antiretroviral therapy for HIV, anti‑TB drugs for TB meningitis, antimalarials for cerebral malaria
GBS: intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) 2 g/kg over 5 days or plasma exchange; IVIG preferred where exchange not feasible
MS/ADEM: high‑dose methylprednisolone 1 g/day for 3‑5 days (if steroids available)
Nutritional: parenteral or high‑dose oral B12 (cyanocobalamin) weekly until levels normalize
Supportive: physiotherapy, bladder training, pain control with gabapentin, monitor respiratory function (spirometry) in GBS

sections.p: Long‑term monitoring prevents relapse and disability.
b: Schedule neurologic review every 3‑6 months; repeat MRI if disease activity suspected
Monitor B12 levels quarterly in deficient patients
Vaccinate against influenza and pneumococcus to reduce infection‑related relapses
Educate on safe herbal use; avoid nitrous oxide exposure
Axonal neuropathy (e.g., diabetic neuropathy) – preserved conduction velocity
Myopathy – proximal weakness with normal reflexes
Stroke – sudden focal deficit without progressive demyelination
Normal MRI early in GBS (peripheral disease) – do not rule out demyelination
Mild B12 deficiency may have normal hemoglobin; rely on MMA
CSF protein may be normal in early GBS; repeat if suspicion persists

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly worsening weakness or breathing difficulty

faq.q: Why does demyelination slow nerve conduction?
faq.a: Myelin provides salt‑bridge insulation; loss forces the impulse to travel continuously, increasing capacitance and reducing speed.

faq.q: Can vitamin B12 deficiency cause spinal cord demyelination?
faq.a: Yes, it produces subacute combined degeneration affecting dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts.

faq.q: Is IVIG always available for GBS in low‑resource settings?
faq.a: If IVIG is unavailable, plasma exchange is the alternative; if neither is possible, focus on respiratory support and physiotherapy.

exam: A 22‑year‑old presents with optic neuritis and limb weakness – what is the next diagnostic step and why? — Order MRI to look for demyelinating lesions; it distinguishes MS from infectious causes.
A patient with recent diarrhoea develops ascending weakness and areflexia – which test confirms GBS and what result is expected? — CSF analysis; elevated protein >0.5 g/L with normal cell count.

In a malnourished adult with peripheral neuropathy, which laboratory test is most specific for B12‑related demyelination? — Serum methylmalonic acid; elevation confirms functional B12 deficiency even if serum B12 is borderline.

A child with cerebral malaria shows seizures and MRI shows diffuse white‑matter hyperintensities – how does malaria cause demyelination? — Cytokine‑mediated inflammation and microvascular injury disrupt myelin integrity.

You suspect TB meningitis causing spinal cord demyelination but MRI is unavailable – what bedside investigation helps and what would you look for? — CSF analysis; high protein, low glucose, lymphocytic pleocytosis, and positive GeneXpert.

A patient on nitrous oxide abuse presents with gait ataxia – which vitamin deficiency explains the myelin damage and how would you treat? — Vitamin B12 deficiency; give parenteral cyanocobalamin after confirming low B12 or elevated MMA.
During GBS management, why might you avoid high‑dose steroids? — Steroids have not shown benefit and may increase infection risk; IVIG or plasma exchange are evidence‑based.
What red‑flag symptom in a demyelinating disease mandates immediate referral to a neurologist? — Rapid respiratory decline or bulbar weakness indicating impending respiratory failure.
